criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains the majority-class-baseline argument (a trivial negative predictor reaches ~99.5%), correctly defines/uses precision and recall, and accurately recommends PR-based evaluation over ROC/accuracy for heavy imbalance. Proposed remedies (class weights, SMOTE/resampling, threshold tuning) are technically valid and correctly applied. Full marks require no incorrect claims (e.g. mixing up precision and recall, or claiming ROC-AUC is unaffected by imbalance).

Covers all three required parts: (1) why accuracy misleads, (2) better metrics with justification, and (3) at least two concrete remedies. Full marks also mention the correct evaluation hygiene (resample only training data, keep a stratified/realistic test distribution). Partial credit if one part is missing or only a single remedy is given.

Explicitly connects the metric choice and threshold to the business cost of false negatives vs false positives and names the precision/recall trade-off as a decision the team must make, rather than just listing techniques. Full marks tie the 'why' of each recommendation to the imbalance and the fraud context.

Well-organized review-style explanation using correct terminology; distinguishes precision from recall clearly and states recommendations a teammate could act on. Deduct for vague, disorganized, or jargon-dropping answers that never explain the reasoning.

expected_answer_points: A trivial classifier that always predicts the majority class ("not fraud") already achieves ~99.5% accuracy, so accuracy merely reflects the base rate and says nothing about fraud-detection ability
Recommends minority-class-focused metrics: precision, recall, and F1 (and the confusion matrix), rather than overall accuracy
Recommends the precision-recall curve / PR-AUC and notes it is more informative than ROC-AUC under severe imbalance (ROC-AUC can look deceptively high because true negatives dominate)

Names the precision vs recall trade-off explicitly and ties it to business cost of false negatives (missed fraud) vs false positives (blocking legitimate customers), which also drives threshold choice
Remedy: cost-sensitive learning / class weights (e.g. class_weight="balanced")
Remedy: resampling the training set (e.g. SMOTE oversampling of the minority or undersampling the majority) and/or tuning the decision threshold away from 0.5
Insists resampling/threshold tuning happen only on training data and the test set preserve the true class distribution (stratified split), so reported metrics reflect production
common_pitfalls: Accepting or defending the 99.5% accuracy, or failing to point out that an always-'not-fraud' baseline already achieves it
Recommending ROC-AUC as the primary metric without recognizing that the precision-recall curve is more informative under extreme imbalance, or asserting ROC-AUC is immune to class imbalance
Applying SMOTE/oversampling (or threshold tuning) to the whole dataset before the train/test split, or resampling the test set, which leaks information and inflates reported metrics
Only listing resampling and forgetting other levers such as class weights / cost-sensitive learning and decision-threshold tuning
Maximizing recall with no regard for the resulting false positives, ignoring the precision/recall trade-off and the business cost of blocking legitimate customers
Confusing or swapping the definitions of precision and recall
reference_answer:
Accuracy is meaningless here because the classes are extremely imbalanced. A trivial model that predicts "not fraud" for every transaction already scores 99.5% accuracy, so that number just reflects the 0.5% base rate and tells us nothing about whether the model catches fraud. I'd ask to see the confusion matrix and minority-class metrics: precision (of the transactions we flag, how many are truly fraud) and recall (of all actual fraud, how much we catch), summarized as F1, and ideally the precision-recall curve / PR-AUC, which is far more informative than ROC-AUC under severe imbalance because ROC is dominated by the huge true-negative count and can look deceptively strong.

The core trade-off the team must decide is recall vs precision, driven by business cost: a false negative is missed fraud (expensive), while a false positive blocks a legitimate customer (annoying, support cost). That decision also sets the operating threshold rather than a default 0.5.

Concrete remedies: (1) cost-sensitive learning via class weights, e.g. class_weight="balanced", so the loss penalizes minority errors more; (2) resampling the training data, e.g. SMOTE oversampling of the minority or undersampling the majority; and (3) tuning the decision threshold on a validation set. Crucially, resampling and threshold tuning must be done only on training folds, and the test set must keep the true 0.5% distribution (stratified split) so the reported metrics reflect production reality.
